Review Text: I, like many shoppers, avoided Temu for years because I wasn't sure if it was legitimate. I now regret that. It just leads to returns of items for refunds when you get something that is not the dimensions you need. I'm going to continue to use Temu. I hear people say they're Communist and they steal your data, and all this and that, but I figure data stealing is probably happening with anything I buy from anybody online, and I'm certainly not going to stop shopping online, the economic benefits are too good.

Review Title: Occasionally good, mostly awful
Review Text:
Ive used Temu a few times, you can get some decent items from there. It's a chinse marketplace, so you get knockoff goods, some poor quality stuff, but also get access to some decent stuff too, at prices which are reasonable.

Any problems, and returns and refunds are simple.

Until they're not. I recent bought an item that was not as described at all, and went to complain. I was offered a £10 voucher, which could be used to take the price off any £10 spend. Thats ANY spend.

I accepted it. It was £3 less than my items value, but i was able to keep the item (which i have since binned because it was more useless than i thought). So I checked some items I wanted, added them to my basket. Knowing there was a £15 minimum spend. I got £15 of items... and got told I still needed to spend £10. Because my voucher removes the payment BEFORE checkout, so checkout does not meet £15.

Bit of a scam for a refund aint it? my refund of £10, is now locked behind me needed to buy £25 of items, and spend £15 of my own money. So I have to give them 150% MORE than my refund, to get my "goodwill apology"

I complained, and got given an upgraded £15 credit voucher.

Which I added, and went to my basket... now I need to spend £15 more. because my voucher wiped out before checkout again. So its not credit, its a scam to get me to give them more money.

I explained this again, and how I'm pretty sure that offering a refund that is then paywalled, must break some sort of laws. I got sent a breakdown of how lucky I am to receive offers and coupons from them, and they're sad that my coupon didnt meant my expectations, but to keep looking out as they give new coupons daily. Again, this was not a bonus coupon, it was meant to be a refund! I told them again, and got told sadly there is nothing they can do.

I now have no coupon (timed out whilst waiting for an answer, because you only have 48 hours to use the refund coupon, probably to force you to rush into a nonsense purchase) and I cant refund the item anymore, because it's already been processed for its one off bonus refund (which was the lame voucher)and even if i could, once I was told to keep the item and I'd get the voucher, the item was binned

Like I said, I've had good experiences with the company. Plenty of useful items for the house, that are genuinely cheaper than other options. But this experience has just left me uninstalling the app, not that its stopped them from sending me 10 texts and whatsapp messages daily.

Review Title: Spotify is a vGreat for listeners, frustrating for independent artistsery strong platform from…
Review Text:
Spotify is a very strong platform from a listener’s perspective: it is convenient, easy to use, offers a huge music library, and has become one of the main places where people discover and listen to music.

From the perspective of an independent artist, however, my experience is much more disappointing. Spotify gives the impression of reach and visibility, but in practice very little of that turns into real support or sustainable growth. Streams generate extremely low income, older achievements quickly lose visibility, follower numbers feel unstable, and without additional marketing money almost nothing happens.

The problem is not Spotify alone, but the whole system around it. Artists create the music, invest time, money and energy, while platforms, distributors, labels and marketing services benefit far more from the structure. For independent musicians, this can easily become frustrating: you keep working, hoping and investing, but the system rarely gives much back.

For listeners, Spotify is excellent. For independent artists, it can be deeply discouraging, unfair and exhausting.

Review Title: Why Am I Paying for Premium?
Review Text:
I’ve been a Spotify Premium subscriber for quite a while, and overall I’ve never had issues with my payments, billing, or music streaming experience. Compared to some of the reviews I’ve seen from other users, my account itself has functioned well.
 However, my biggest frustration is with podcasts and the way ads are still delivered throughout episodes, even while paying for Premium.
I understand the difference between Spotify platform ads and ads embedded directly by podcast creators, but from a customer perspective, “Premium” and “ad-free” create the expectation of uninterrupted listening. Instead, podcast episodes are still constantly interrupted by host-read sponsorships and promotional segments.
 Music playback is mostly excellent, but the podcast experience feels misleading when paying customers still have to manually skip through ads and sponsored interruptions. If Spotify markets Premium as an ad-free experience, there should be clearer communication about what that actually means for podcast listeners.
 I’m not asking for perfection. I just want the uninterrupted listening experience I believed I was paying for.

I am currently in an ongoing dispute with Booking.com over a £280.50 refund that I was explicitly promised but have not received.

This was not presented to me as a voucher, reward or credit towards a future booking. I was told it would be a refund.

I specifically sought confirmation of this and was told by a Booking.com representative:

“I have already coordinated with our senior team and received approval for the full coverage of your price difference.”

I was then told that, in order for Booking.com to “process the refund”, I needed to complete my stay and provide an invoice from the property showing a zero balance.

The representative also explicitly assured me:

“For now, I can assure you that we will cover the entire amount of the difference.”

I relied on those assurances and followed Booking.com’s instructions exactly. I completed the stay, obtained the required zero-balance invoice and submitted it to them.

The price difference was £280.50.

I expected the refund I had been promised.

Instead, Booking.com placed £280.50 into my Booking.com Wallet as Travel Credits.

I do not accept these Travel Credits as fulfilment of the promised refund, and I am still seeking the return of my £280.50.

This is not simply a technical difference in how the money has been processed.

My Booking.com Wallet specifically shows £280.50 in Travel Credits and £0 in Cash Credits. I cannot withdraw the £280.50 to my bank account or payment card. It can only be used towards future Booking.com purchases, and even then only on bookings that accept Wallet payments. The credit also has an expiry date.

That is materially different from refunding £280.50 to me.

It effectively requires me to spend the value through Booking.com in the future rather than returning the money that I was told would be refunded.

Had Booking.com originally offered me £280.50 of restricted Travel Credit, that would have been a different proposition entirely. But that is not what I agreed to and not what I was promised.

I was told that senior-team approval had already been received for the full coverage of the price difference. I was told my invoice was required to process the refund. I was assured that Booking.com would cover the entire amount of the difference.

I complied with the condition Booking.com set on the basis of those assurances.

Since discovering that the £280.50 had been issued as Travel Credits rather than refunded, I have repeatedly tried to get Booking.com to correct this and honour what I was promised.

I have contacted customer service, followed up by email and contacted Booking.com through social media. I have made clear that I am disputing the Travel Credits and want the £280.50 refunded as originally promised.

I am still waiting for Booking.com to resolve this.

My follow-up communications have not resulted in a meaningful response, and I have not been able to establish that my complaint has even been formally logged and progressed through a proper complaints process.

As Booking.com has so far failed to resolve the matter directly with me, I have now initiated a dispute with my bank in an attempt to recover the £280.50.

That bank dispute is ongoing too.

Fortunately, I retained evidence throughout this process. I have screenshots confirming the senior-team approval, Booking.com’s use of the word “refund”, the assurance that the “entire amount” would be covered, evidence that I supplied the invoice they requested, and screenshots of my Wallet showing £280.50 in Travel Credits and £0 in Cash Credits.

To be completely clear: the fact that Booking.com has placed £280.50 of Travel Credits in my account does not mean this matter has been resolved.

I have not accepted restricted Travel Credits as a substitute for the refund I was promised.

I am still seeking the £280.50 refund in money, and this dispute remains ongoing.

I will update this review if Booking.com resolves the matter.

Until then, my advice to anyone dealing with Booking.com customer service is to keep screenshots of absolutely everything you are promised in writing. I’m very glad I did.

Review Text:
Booking.com is fine until something goes wrong — never again

After two separate experiences where Booking.com failed us when we actually needed their help, I will never use Booking.com again.

The first occurred on a trip to Madeira. I specifically purchased and paid for an ocean-view room through Booking.com. When we arrived, we were given a terrible room with no ocean view. It felt like a bait-and-switch — the room we received was not what I had purchased.

I don't blame Booking.com for a typhoon or an airline cancelling flights. I also understand that hotels make mistakes. What matters to me is what the company I booked through does when something goes wrong.

And that is where Booking.com has failed us — twice.

The contrast with my experiences using Expedia could not be greater. I have also encountered travel problems with Expedia, but when I needed help, Expedia stood behind me 100%. That is what I expect from a company I trust with my travel arrangements.

I'm not giving up on online travel agencies. I'm giving up on Booking.com.

Two serious problems on two different trips. Two opportunities for Booking.com to stand behind its customer. Twice they failed us.

Review Title: Paid extra for Flexible Tickets, but rebooking costs more than buying new flights
Review Text:
I am extremely dissatisfied with Booking.com / Gotogate.

When I originally booked my flights, I paid an additional £13 per passenger for the Flexible Ticket option, specifically so that I could change my travel dates without paying amendment or rebooking fees, with only any fare difference payable if applicable.

I am travelling with two passengers, so I paid extra specifically for this flexibility.

Now I need to change my London–Rome and Rome–London flights, and Gotogate is asking me to pay approximately £128 to amend my existing tickets.

However, I have documented evidence showing that completely new return tickets for the required dates can be purchased for substantially less. At one point I found the new return journey for around £49, and I also have a current Booking.com quotation showing £90 total for two travellers, including taxes and fees.

Even more importantly, the replacement fare itself was lower than the fare I originally paid, meaning the fare difference was effectively negative.

So I paid extra for a Flexible Ticket advertised as allowing changes without amendment fees, yet when I actually try to use it, I am being asked to pay £128 even though the replacement flights are cheaper than my original booking and cheaper to buy again as completely new tickets.

This makes absolutely no sense to me.

I repeatedly asked customer service to provide a transparent breakdown explaining exactly how the £128 charge was calculated, including the fare difference, airline amendment fees and any other charges.

I have not received a satisfactory explanation.

In my opinion, this makes the Flexible Ticket product extremely difficult to justify. I paid extra in advance specifically to avoid rebooking fees, but when I actually need to use the flexibility I purchased, the cost of amending the tickets is higher than simply abandoning them and purchasing new flights.

I have now raised a formal dispute with Clearpay and supplied supporting evidence, including screenshots of the rebooking quotation, current replacement fares and my communications with Booking.com / Gotogate.

If this matter is not resolved satisfactorily, I will consider escalating the payment dispute further through my card issuer.

My advice to other customers is simple: be extremely careful before paying extra for the Flexible Ticket option through Gotogate / Booking.com.

Based on my experience, the practical benefit of this product is very questionable when a customer can apparently be charged more to amend an existing ticket than to buy an entirely new one.

Review Title: I would avoid this company at all…
Review Text:
I would avoid this company at all costs.

A phishing link was sent to me through Booking.com's own messaging system, and it took me finding the evidence myself to get anyone to act

I booked a London apartment through Booking.com for August. After I confirmed the reservation, a message came through Booking.com's own platform directing me to an external website to enter my card details. Booking.com's published guidance is that they never ask guests to do this.

What I then found, entirely on my own:

1. The contact number given for a London property was a US number.
2. The host did not respond for four days, not to my messages, not to Booking.com's messages, and not to a phone call Booking.com made to them.

4. The Booking.com listing page for the property is titled as a holiday cottage in Somerset, not the London apartment I had booked.

1. I was given three different timeframes in a single day. First 48 hours, then three hours, then no timeframe at all.
2. A live chat was closed on me while I still had unanswered questions.
3. One agent confirmed in writing that relocation would be arranged free of charge. A second agent confirmed relocation was guaranteed. A third then told me the approved support was €25.

5. The alternative eventually offered was student accommodation in zone 4, priced below my original booking so that Booking.com contributed nothing at all.
6. Any shortfall would be paid as Travel Credits to spend with Booking.com, not as money.

Fraudulent listings appear on every large platform. That is not the problem. The problem is that a phishing attempt was delivered through Booking.com's own systems, that the listing did not match its own page, that none of it was detected until a customer did the work, and that the response was to offer €25 and a suggestion I pay for it myself.

I have retained the complete documentary evidence, including:

• the original 7-seat confirmation;
• the later 5-seat voucher;
• the full live chat transcript;
• and Booking.com’s written acknowledgements that the booking no longer matches the original confirmation.

At present, however, I cannot recommend using Booking.com for car hire where vehicle specifications are critical.

Review Title: Avoid Gotogate by Booking.com at All Costs
Review Text:
My experience with Gotogate by Booking.com has been one of the most frustrating and stressful travel experiences I've ever had. I strongly advise anyone considering booking through them to think twice.

Our Thai Lion Air flight was cancelled by the airline on 3 June, well in advance of our scheduled travel on 2 July. However, we were never informed by Gotogate or Booking.com that our flight had been cancelled. There was no email, no SMS, no phone call, and no attempt to offer an alternative flight or assist us in any way.

The only reason we discovered the cancellation was when we tried to complete web check-in before our trip. Imagine the shock and panic of finding out that your flight doesn't even exist just days before your vacation. Because of this complete failure in communication, we were forced to book expensive last-minute replacement tickets, costing us significantly more than what we had originally paid.

The worst part began after that. It has now been over two months, and despite countless follow-ups, we have still not received our refund. Every single time we contact Gotogate, we are given the same scripted response: "We are waiting for the airline to refund us." They refuse to take any ownership of the issue or provide any meaningful update.

To make matters worse, they repeatedly provide incorrect information, claiming that the flight was cancelled on 3 July, when in reality it was cancelled on 3 June. Even after correcting them multiple times, they continue to rely on inaccurate records instead of investigating the matter properly.

As the company that accepted my payment and issued my booking, Gotogate/Booking.com should be accountable to their customers. Passing all responsibility to the airline while leaving customers without information, assistance, or refunds is simply unacceptable. Customers should not be expected to bear the financial burden and uncertainty because an intermediary fails to do its job.

The entire experience has caused unnecessary financial loss, countless hours spent chasing customer support, and tremendous mental stress. Every interaction has felt like talking to a wall, with no accountability, no empathy, and no resolution.

I have completely lost trust in Gotogate and Booking.com for flight bookings. Saving a small amount on a ticket is not worth the risk of being abandoned when something goes wrong.

My advice to anyone considering booking flights through Gotogate or Booking.com: Don't. Book directly with the airline or use a travel agency that actually supports its customers. If your flight gets cancelled, be prepared for poor communication, endless excuses, delayed refunds, and zero accountability.

This has been one of the worst customer service experiences I have ever had, and I will never use Gotogate or Booking.com for flight bookings again. I will also actively recommend that my friends, family, and colleagues avoid them if they value their money, time, and peace of mind.

Review Title: Booking.com is a terrible platform
Review Text:
Booking.com is a terrible platform that had repeatedly failed me when I needed customer service

I have used Booking.com extensively, but my experience following a serious incident at a property has completely changed my view of the company.

I booked four nights at Westbury House in Windermere through Booking.com. I physically attended the property within the stated check-in period, with my luggage, and attempted to check in. Following an extraordinary confrontation with the owners, the door was closed on me while I was still standing at the threshold. I was not admitted and received none of the four nights I had paid for.

What happened afterwards with Booking.com was almost as appalling.

I spent approximately two hours making around 16 calls to Booking.com numbers in Australia, the UK and the Netherlands trying to report what had happened. Calls repeatedly disconnected, including after I had been placed on hold, meaning I had to call back, identify myself and start explaining everything again.

One agent, Mohammed, became embroiled in a pointless argument about my reservation number, despite ultimately acknowledging that he could already identify the booking. When I asked for a supervisor, he refused to escalate the call.

I called again and spoke with Christine. After I criticised the lack of empathy and customer service I was receiving, she actually told me:

“I’m hanging up on you. You have to call back. I don’t like the way you’re speaking to me.”

And she did.

Meanwhile, Booking.com was emailing me saying it had contacted the property about my complaint even though nobody had successfully taken my complete account of what had happened. I replied asking, “How can you have advised them when I have not told you a thing?” and repeatedly asked for someone to call me.

I then pursued Booking.com through email and X/Twitter, including providing a detailed written account. I was repeatedly redirected back towards the same telephone customer-service system that had already failed me.

Now comes perhaps the most disturbing part: despite my repeatedly telling Booking.com that I physically attended Westbury House and had the door closed on me at the threshold, I have apparently been recorded as a NO-SHOW.

That is simply false.

And conveniently, being classified as a no-show means I am now unable to leave a Booking.com review of the property and what happened to me there.

So I attended the property, was refused the accommodation, spent hours trying to report what happened, experienced repeated disconnections and failed escalation, sent written complaints explaining that I had attended — and I am now prevented from reviewing the property because the booking records incorrectly say I never showed up.

Whether Booking.com or the property disputes my entitlement to a refund is one issue. Whether I attended the property is another. I did attend. I was not a no-show.

A booking platform proves its value when something goes wrong. Taking a reservation and processing payment is easy. Providing meaningful assistance when a customer is standing outside accommodation they have paid for is where customer service actually matters.

In my experience, Booking.com failed spectacularly at precisely that point.

Review Title: Promised a refund, now being offered Travel Credit
Review Text:
Extremely disappointing experience with Booking.com.

We booked an apartment in Nice but were informed there was a leak and were offered an alternative apartment further away from the city centre. We said we wanted to keep that option open while seeing whether something closer was available. Instead, our booking was cancelled, leaving us without accommodation and having to spend a considerable amount of time contacting Booking.com.

When we eventually spoke to a representative, we were told we could choose alternative accommodation and that Booking.com would refund the difference in price.

We selected more expensive accommodation in the centre and then received written confirmation from Booking.com stating:

“We will cover up the price difference up to the amount EUR 336.39.”

Based on both the telephone conversation and this written confirmation, we booked the more expensive accommodation, which cost €882.96. We would not have chosen accommodation at this price had we not been assured that Booking.com would cover the difference.

After our stay, Booking.com asked us to provide an invoice in order to process the reimbursement. Their subsequent email repeatedly referred to this as a refund, including:

“To proceed with your refund request…”

“We’ll be happy to move forward with your refund.”

And most clearly:

“Once we receive this, we will promptly process the refund for you.”

Despite all of this, we are now being told that the price difference will NOT be refunded and can only be provided as Booking.com Travel Credit towards a future booking.

What makes this even more frustrating is that Booking.com clearly knows the distinction between a refund and Travel Credit. In the original email, they separately stated that if we incurred “additional charges at the new place”, they could “look into adding Travel Credits to your Wallet.”

Travel Credits were therefore specifically mentioned in relation to additional charges, but NOT when Booking.com told us they would “cover” the price difference. We were also verbally told it would be a refund and subsequently received an email referring to the payment as a “refund” multiple times.

Had we been told from the outset that we would have to pay the additional cost ourselves and receive credit towards a future Booking.com reservation instead, we would NEVER have chosen the more expensive accommodation.

Customer service throughout this process has also been incredibly frustrating. Telephone waiting times are very long, getting through to someone who can actually help is extremely difficult, and we have even had calls cut off after waiting, forcing us to start the process again.

We aren't asking for anything extra. We simply want Booking.com to honour what we were repeatedly told, both verbally and in writing, and reimburse the agreed price difference, up to the €336.39 maximum confirmed in their email.

Travel Credit requiring us to book with Booking.com again is not the same as the refund we were repeatedly told we would receive.

I will happily update this review if Booking.com honours the reimbursement we were promised and resolves the matter.

Review Title: PayPal and "Linked Payments"
Review Text:
I have been a long-time, albeit small, user of PayPal and have generally been very happy with the service until recently.

Since the introduction of “linked accounts”, I have experienced confusing problems when sending money. PayPal appears to accept the transaction and indicates that the money has been sent to the recipient, but it does not make it sufficiently clear that the recipient may need to take further action to confirm or accept the payment.

The recipient, who is not expecting to have to do this, can understandably believe that the money has not been sent. Worse, from their perspective, it can appear that the sender is claiming to have sent money when nothing has actually been received, which can make a legitimate transaction look suspicious or even fraudulent.

This is an unnecessarily confusing process for both the sender and recipient, and PayPal's communication around it is inadequate. In my view, PayPal has made what should be a simple process unnecessarily complicated.

After this experience, I have lost confidence in PayPal and will no longer use the service.

Review Title: PayPal Purchase Protection Failed Me When I Needed It
Review Text:
I used PayPal because I believed their Purchase Protection would protect me if I paid for something and never received it. Unfortunately, that was not my experience.

I purchased a shirt from a company I found through a Facebook ad and never received it. The seller claimed the package had been delivered and even stated that it had been “signed for,” but I did not sign for anything and was home at the time the package was supposedly delivered.

The tracking information was vague. It showed the package as delivered to my town, but did not identify the actual last-mile carrier or provide verifiable proof that it was delivered to my address. I repeatedly asked the seller for proof of delivery, including the alleged signature, but they never provided it.

I opened a PayPal dispute and provided documentation and an explanation of what happened. The seller's only response was that the order had been “signed for,” without providing any supporting evidence. PayPal initially closed the case in the seller's favor less than a few hours after I escalated it. I appealed the decision, and the appeal was also denied in the seller's favor in less than two days. Neither decision provided a meaningful explanation of what evidence was relied upon or any proof that the package was actually delivered to my address.

What is most disappointing is that I never felt that the actual question — whether this package was delivered to me — was adequately addressed. I was left with the seller's unsupported claim that it had been delivered, while I never received the merchandise.

I used PayPal specifically because I believed I was getting an additional layer of protection as a buyer. Based on this experience, I would not rely on PayPal's Purchase Protection for an item-not-received dispute where the seller simply claims that tracking shows delivery.

Based on our experience, we would not recommend PayPal as a payment provider for businesses that rely on timely access to their operating funds.

Review Title: PayPal Suspends Digital Payments for Months Under Undefined “Security Review” Documented Evidence Inside
Review Text:
As an independent type designer selling digital fonts, my business relies on instant and reliable payment processing. Unfortunately, my experience with PayPal has repeatedly shown that their system is neither reliable nor transparent. Over the past year, I have encountered multiple cases where PayPal suspended perfectly legitimate credit‑card purchases under the vague label of "Security Review." This term is never clearly defined in PayPal's user agreement, and in practice it seems to be used as a blanket justification for freezing funds without explanation, without communication, and without any actionable steps for either the merchant or the customer.
One of the most concerning examples occurred in April 2026, when a customer purchased a €24 digital font from my store. The payment was immediately placed under "security review," and neither I nor the customer had access to the funds. The customer's bank confirmed the charge, yet PayPal did not release the payment to me, nor did they refund it to the customer. The transaction remained in limbo for three full months, with no updates, no human support, and no ability to file a dispute because PayPal's Resolution Center repeatedly displayed technical errors across multiple devices. Eventually, PayPal quietly reversed the payment and sent it back to the customer-three months later-without any explanation of what "security" required such an excessive delay.
This is not an isolated incident. I recently experienced another suspended payment where the customer believed I had received her money, while PayPal showed the transaction as "Pending" and provided no way to accept, cancel, or refund it. As a digital‑goods seller, this places me in an impossible position: my website cannot release download links until payment is confirmed, yet PayPal's opaque review process makes me appear as though I am withholding the customer's purchase. This damages my reputation, creates unnecessary conflict with clients, and disrupts my business operations.
PayPal's lack of human support is a major part of the problem. There is no accessible customer‑service email for Europe, phone calls go unanswered, and the automated chat provides no real assistance. When PayPal freezes a payment, both merchant and customer are left without any recourse. The company's communication consists of generic messages asking us to "wait," even when the delay lasts days, weeks, or-as in my documented case-months.
Based on my experience, PayPal's "security review" appears less like a protective measure and more like an internal process that allows the company to hold funds in a suspended state without accountability. While I cannot speak to PayPal's internal motives, the practical effect is clear: money is locked between the bank and PayPal, inaccessible to both merchant and customer, while PayPal benefits from holding large volumes of pending transactions. For small independent merchants, this is not security-it is a systemic failure that undermines trust and disrupts business.
I am sharing this detailed account, supported by screenshots, transaction IDs, and correspondence, so other digital‑goods sellers and customers understand the risks of relying on PayPal. My hope is that PayPal will address these issues, improve transparency, and provide real human support. Until then, I cannot recommend PayPal as a reliable payment processor for digital products.

Review Title: My experience with PayPal has been extremely disappointing.
Review Text:
My experience with PayPal has been extremely disappointing.

On 26 July 2026, my mobile phone was stolen in London. Within a very short period, the thief gained unauthorised access to my PayPal account, applied for PayPal Credit and made three purchases totalling £3,597.

I immediately reported the theft to Vodafone, HSBC, Revolut and the Metropolitan Police (Crime Reference 01/7864424/26).

I contacted PayPal as soon as I became aware of the fraud. My first claim was rejected without any meaningful explanation. I then spent over an hour on the phone to another adviser who repeatedly assured me that I was fully protected against fraud, told me she “had my back”, and promised all three transactions would be reversed. Relieved, I ended the call believing the matter had been resolved.

Later that same night I received another automated email saying my claim had been rejected again.

What concerns me most is that nobody has been able to explain why. I have been passed between different departments, nobody can tell me why the claim was rejected, and nobody will transfer me to the team that made the decision.

One of the fraudulent orders was placed with Argos under the name “Anwar Elmi” for collection at a location in Colindale—a person and location that have absolutely no connection to me. Despite providing this information, along with my police crime reference and evidence that my phone had been stolen, it appears not to have been properly considered.

I also cannot understand how PayPal Credit could allegedly be opened and used to spend £3,597 within such a short period after my phone was stolen without additional verification, yet PayPal concluded this was authorised activity.

I have now had to submit an identity theft claim through PayPal Credit while remaining liable for thousands of pounds of debt created by a criminal.

I hope PayPal reviews this matter properly because, so far, the handling of my case has left me with very little confidence in their fraud investigation process.

Review Title: They froze my business funds for no reason, then let a six-year-old spend $400, then pointed at the bank, and the merchant.
Review Text:
Start with the part that should matter most to anyone running a company. PayPal froze funds in my business account with no explanation I ever received.

Not a fraud alert I could resolve, not a documentation request I could satisfy. Money I earned, held, on their timeline, for reasons they did not explain.

I used them for merchant services. I will never route a dollar of business volume through them again, and I will not recommend them to another operator.

The consumer side is what finally ended it.

On June 19, 2026, my account absorbed eight-plus consecutive charges from a single merchant inside a few minutes. They ran from $0.99 to $99.99 and totaled roughly $400. Three of them were near $100 apiece: $99.99, $99.99, and $94.99. Every one of them was my six-year-old tapping buttons in a mobile game.

Not one triggered a verification prompt. Not the fifth charge. Not the eighth. Not three separate hits at around a hundred dollars each.

A rapid burst of mixed micro and macro transactions from one merchant on one device in one sitting is a textbook velocity pattern, the exact thing a payments risk engine exists to catch.

Theirs caught nothing.

Then came the shell game. I filed an unauthorized transaction dispute, which is the product PayPal advertises.

The merchant said they could no longer refund because PayPal controlled the case. PayPal declined to make me whole and directed me to my card issuer, Barclays.

Barclays told me PayPal should have squared it away, because PayPal is the entity that processed the transactions and holds the relationship with the merchant.

Three companies, one $400 hole, and every one of them insisting the responsibility sits somewhere else.

That is the whole product. PayPal collects a fee to stand between you and the merchant, and the instant something goes wrong it becomes a pass-through pipe with no responsibility for what flowed through it.

A card used directly gives you chargeback rights with actual teeth. PayPal gives you a portal and a form letter and a phone number for someone else.

Years as a customer, on both the consumer and merchant side. One afternoon with a first grader and a screen exposed exactly how thin the protection is.
